newsitem.title: USA: Electric reliability seen helped by deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Electric reliability seen helped by deregulation.

text.p: Deregulation of the U.S. electricity industry will likely enhance system reliability as well as clarify financial responsbility for outages, industry experts said at an Edison Electric Institute conference this week.
"As a result of industry restructuring, we will have regulators overseeing reliability," said William Scherman, former general counsel at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
Stanley Skinner, chairman of San Francisco-based Pacific Gas and Electric Co. said "the focus on grid reliability will be enhanced through restructuring."
In California, he noted, an independent sytem operator (ISO), overseen by a governing board, will replace the current "fragmented system."
The ISO will have authority to require utilities to conduct maintenance and upgrade facilities, Skinner added.

Erle Nye, chief executive officer at Texas Utilities, said "the existing protocols are not adequate for the uses we intend. Economic pressures are causing the industry to make greater use of interconnections than ever before."

He suggested that system operations need to be upgraded, each region should be subject to control by an independent operator and all market participants should be required to comply with the new standards.

In any case, the market will not accept unreliable service, noted James Rogers, chief executive officer of Cinergy Corp. "You are not going to cut costs so close that you can't provide service," he said.
But A.W. Dahlberg, chairman of The Southern Co., cautioned that in the short term, "reliability will suffer a bit. Once systems are integrated reliability will improve, it is pretty darn good now."

Still, the current system of regional reliability councils depends "on a handshake and a brotherhood," said Carol Guthrie, an area manager with Chevron's energy services group. "If an operator fails to pick up the phone and tell other utilities that a tree has fallen on a power line, there are no financial or other consequences."

She was referring to circumstances surrounding the August 10 power outage which began on lines operated by the Bonneville Power Administration in the Northwest, but which quickly spread through several western states.
"We are looking forward to the day when we can iron out what reliability really is," she added. "Right now there is no definition of what constitutes an incident (of electric failure)."
